newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O.Licht 2nd estimate of World Coffee Production.
newsitem.headline: F.O.Licht 2nd estimate of World Coffee Production.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.
SECOND ESTIMATE OF WORLD COFFEE PRODUCTION 1996/97 (CROP YEARS)
First figure 1996/97, second figure 1995/96, figures in brackets previous estimate (November 26, 1996), all figures in 1,000 bags green bean.
World coffee production 97621/87679 (96453) World arabica production 65054/57970 (64780) World robusta production 32567/29709 (31673)

Arabica production: Ethiopia 4100/3800, Kenya 1333/1534, Africa total 7484/7615 (7518), Costa Rica 2700/2606, El Salvador 2450/2453, Guatemala 3623/3873, Honduras 2000/1911, Mexico 4995/5231, North and Central America total 18493/18984 (17734), Brazil 22750/11300, Colombia 9600/12890, Peru 1450/1446, Venezuela 1060/1250, South America total 35991/28083 (36355), India 1499/1720, Indonesia 520/406, Asia total 2110/2200 (2197), Oceania total 976/1088 (976).

Robusta production: Ivory Coast 4500/2900, Uganda 3420/3923, Africa total 11414/9895 (10189), North and Central America total 231/229 (256), Brazil 5750/4500, South America total 6500/5295 (5945), India 1500/1996, Indonesia 5980/5942, Thailand 1312/1313, Vietnam 4467/3917, Asia total 14365/14238 (15226), Oceania total 57/52 (57).

World coffee production in 1996/97 is now forecast to amount to 97.6 mn bags. This compares with the figure of 96.5 mn bags at which it was put in November. Most of the increase is in the robusta sector which is now forecast to reach 32.6 mn bags against the November figure of 31.7 mn bags. At 65 mn bags the arabica total is only marginally higher than was forecast in November.

African output is expected to reach nearly 19 mn bags this season. Robusta coffee is expected to account for about 60 per cent of the total with arabica at 40 per cent. Forecasts of output in the Cote d'Ivoire range from 3.8 to 5.0 mn bags. This is a big jump against last season but wastage and rejection will limit exports. With 4.1 mn bags Ethiopia will be the second highest producer in Africa. Here again it should be noted that there is still a wide range between official and trade estimates.

In North and Central America output is now put at 18.7 mn bags, up from 18.0 mn bags forecast in November but still lower than last season's 19.2 mn bags. Almost all the coffee produced in this region is arabica. At 5.15 mn bags Mexico is by far the largest producer in the region even though, reflecting the biannual production cycle, it is down by 250,000 bags on the year. There are plans to reach a total of 8.0 mn bags by 2000. Because of NAFTA Mexico is in a strategic position to expand exports. The setback in Guatemala was not so great as had been forecast and output in 1996/97 is now estimated at 3.65 mn bags against 3.9 mn bags last season.

As always, the Brazilian estimate dominates the South American picture. The total for the continent is about 42.5 mn bags. Brazil, with an increase of 12.7 mn bags over last season's frost and drought damaged crop, is expected to account for 28.5 mn bags or more than two thirds of this. A whole range of problems has hit the Colombian industry and production is expected to fall to 9.6 mn bags from 12.89 mn bags in 1995/96. It is hoped that the steep rise in world market prices will help revive the sector. About 85 per cent of the coffee produced in the region is arabica.

At nearly 16.5 mn bags output in Asia is expected to amount to slightly more than in the previous season. The continent is the largest robusta producing region with 87 per cent of its output being of that type. Statistics from Indonesia, which is the largest producer in the region, vary substantially according to source but output in 1996/97 is expected to reach about 6.5 mn bags, up by about 150,000 bags on the year. Robusta coffee is the predominant variety but there are plans to increase production of arabica and also to expand domestic consumption which is still very low. The industry in Vietnam continues to grow and output is now expected to reach 4.5 mn bags compared with less than 4.0 mn bags in 1995/96 and roughly double what was achieved only four seasons ago. There are plans for a further expansion.

Papua New Guinea, the only important producer in Oceania, is expected to produce about one mn bags in 1996/97, almost all of it arabica. This is slightly lower than in the previous season but the official target is for 1.5 mn bags by the year 2000.

Even though the statistics point to a sharp increase in production in 1996/97 initial consumption forecasts suggest there will be little if any improvement to stocks so that the stock position will remain highly precarious. With a good chance that production will fall in both Brazil and Indonesia next season increases in other producing countries will be needed. A frost in Brazil would be the last drop in the bucket. Highly remunerative prices, especially for arabica producers, appear likely for the remainder of the year.
